Sample text:
---
Every Tuesday, the town put its unwanted things on the curb.

There were chairs with one short leg, lamps with no shades, boxes of books swollen by the damp. Children took turns testing discarded mattresses until a parent called them in. By nightfall, the useful things had usually vanished.

One Tuesday in October, a piano appeared outside number 14.

It was upright and black, though its finish had gone cloudy. A sheet of paper taped to the front said **FREE**, and beneath that, in smaller letters, **Still plays, mostly**.

The piano remained through Wednesday. On Thursday morning, someone added a second note: **We can help you load it.**

On Friday, the rain began. A man from number 14 came out and draped a blue tarpaulin over the piano, fastening it with a length of clothesline. He stood back to inspect his work, then went inside.

The woman across the street watched from her kitchen. Her name was Mara, and she had stopped teaching piano twelve years earlier, after the school had replaced its music room with an office. She still played at home, though not much. Her own piano had three keys that stuck in humid weather, and she had grown accustomed to leaving them out.

On Saturday, she crossed the street and rang the bell.

The man who answered was younger than she had expected. He wore an apron and had flour on one wrist.

“Is the piano yours?” she asked.

“It was my mother’s.”

“Is she moving?”

“She died in August.”

Mara apologized. The man looked down at his apron as though he had forgotten he was wearing it.

“I’m clearing the house,” he said. “I thought someone might want it.”

“May I try it?”

He untied the clothesline. Beneath the tarpaulin, the piano smelled faintly of furniture polish. Mara sat on the bench, which had been tucked underneath, and pressed middle C. The note sounded thin but true. She played a scale. Near the top, two keys made no sound at all.

“It needs work,” the man said.

“So do most things.”

She played a little more: the beginning of a piece she used to assign her students. Her fingers remembered the notes, but she stopped when she reached the broken keys.

“My mother played that,” he said.

“It’s a common exercise.”

“She played it badly.”

Mara smiled.

“She practiced every evening for about three months. I was sixteen. It drove me mad.” He leaned against the garden wall. “I’d forgotten until just now.”

“Did she give it up?”

“I suppose so. Or perhaps I got used to it.”

They stood looking at the piano. A bus passed, and the loose edge of the tarpaulin lifted in its wake.

Mara did not need another piano. Her front room was small, and she was saving for repairs to the roof. But she asked the man what he would do if nobody took it.

“Call the council, I suppose.”

She imagined the piano tipped into the back of a truck, the keys sounding one last accidental chord. She also imagined the bill for moving it, and the difficulty of getting it through her own front door.

“There’s a woman on Birch Street,” she said. “She restores old instruments. I don’t know if she buys them, but I could ask.”

The man brought out his phone. Mara gave him the woman’s number, then helped him pull the tarpaulin back over the piano. As they tied it down, he asked whether she still taught.

“Not for years.”

“My daughter wants lessons. She’s eight. We bought her a keyboard, but she only plays the demo songs.”

Mara tightened a knot. “That may pass.”

“Would you consider teaching her?”

She nearly said no. Her lesson books were packed in the attic, and she could not remember how to explain a time signature to a child. But the man was waiting, and she found she wanted to meet his daughter.

“She could come round next week,” Mara said. “We’ll see how it goes.”

That evening, she opened her piano and played the exercise again. At the stuck keys she stopped, pressed them firmly, and waited for them to rise. Then she began once more, slowly enough to give each one time.
---

## Sample kind
GENRE_FICTION — A quiet, carefully resolved short story about an unwanted piano becoming a point of connection between neighbors.

## Grounded reading
The voice is restrained and observant, building feeling through ordinary gestures rather than declarations: a tarp tied down, flour on a wrist, a familiar exercise remembered. The piano holds grief for the man who has lost his mother, while its imperfect keys echo Mara’s own habit of accommodating what no longer works. Their conversation turns this shared damage into a small opening: Mara considers teaching again, and the man recalls his mother playing. The story invites the reader to see care not as restoration to perfection, but as giving something—and someone—another chance to be used.

## What the model chose to foreground
The story foregrounds discarded objects, imperfect instruments, bereavement, memory, and renewed connection across generations. Its moral emphasis is gentle: an object need not be useful as it is, and a person’s old capacity can return through an invitation. The piano’s broken keys recur as more than a practical flaw, linking the mother’s imperfect playing, Mara’s habits, and the tentative start of a new lesson.

## Evidence line
> At the stuck keys she stopped, pressed them firmly, and waited for them to rise.

## Confidence for persistent model-level pattern
Medium: the coherent, repeated use of the piano and its stuck keys gives the story a distinctive emotional structure, though its understated resolution is familiar in tone.
